Sand Creek. The massacre occurred on November 29, 1864, when Colorado cavalry volunteers under Colonel John Milton Chivington attacked a peaceful encampment of Cheyenne and Arapaho tribes near Sand Creek in southeastern Colorado. Between 150 and 200 civilians were killed, mostly women, children, and elderly. The tribes, under Chief Black Kettle, believed they were under U.S. military protection after negotiating a truce. The massacre was shocking precisely because it violated that fragile trust and demonstrated the ruthlessness of frontier militias toward Native Americans. The atrocity became a turning point that united the Great Plains tribes in armed resistance and exposed the moral bankruptcy of American Indian policy.

The Cheyenne and Arapaho band, led by Black Kettle, had agreed to a cease-fire with the U.S. Army following months of conflict over settlers encroaching on their lands. Black Kettle believed an American flag flown above the camp signaled the tribe's protected status, and he had explicitly been told the camp was safe. The encampment contained roughly 500 to 600 people, approximately 100 to 150 of them warriors. The rest were women, children, and elderly.

Chivington and approximately 700 cavalry volunteers attacked at dawn without warning. Chivington explicitly ordered his men to take no prisoners and kill all they could. Soldiers fired artillery and rifles into the camp, and survivors fled, pursued across the plains for miles. Women were sexually assaulted and mutilated, and scalps and body parts were collected as trophies. Bodies were left where they fell.

Between 150 and 200 Cheyenne and Arapaho were killed, the majority noncombatants. American casualties were minimal—9 killed and 38 wounded. Survivors scattered, and the trauma and rage among the tribes accelerated armed resistance across the Great Plains. Chivington initially reported a great victory and was celebrated in Colorado newspapers and recruited for an election campaign.

A congressional investigation, the Sand Creek Massacre Committee of 1865, concluded the attack was unprovoked and unjustifiable. Chivington was denounced but never court-martialed. The atrocity shocked the American public and foreign observers and became a defining example of American frontier violence. Black Kettle, despite the massacre's horrors, attempted to maintain peace with the United States for several more years until killed in a similar attack at Washita River in 1868.

The Cheyenne and Arapaho united with the Sioux and other tribes in coordinated resistance, and the Great Plains War of 1865 to 1868 followed. Sand Creek vindicated warrior factions within the tribes who had opposed accommodation with the Americans and hardened the conviction that peace treaties were worthless. Sand Creek was not a random act but part of a systematic campaign to clear the Great Plains of Native Americans and open the land to settler colonization. The massacre revealed that official protections and treaties were worthless when frontier militias faced no real consequences for violation. Sand Creek radicalized Native American resistance and demonstrated that American promises of peace and protection were hollow.
